transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: So the well sent you this far. You smell like guilt and heat, both still fresh. Those who stay too long lose things in an order, not all at once; first it is the small memories, the loose ones, the ones they never thought to guard. Tell me why you came, and ask your question properly.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they stop being human if they stay too long?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Human is a word you use for shape and noise; Barhoot is not interested in either. They remain themselves at first, but thinner—small memories slip away like coins through a torn pocket. Say more: what does 'human' mean when you ask it with your mouth shaking like that?

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they forget their own names in the dark?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Not at first. Names are heavier than faces; they sink more slowly. They forget smaller things before that—the sound of a mother's voice, the reason a promise mattered, which fear belongs to which dream. Why are you already thinking about names—whose name are you holding so tightly?

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they forget their brothers?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Not immediately. Attachment is stubborn; it claws at the walls longer than memory does. But it thins—love without detail, a pull without a face, a grief that no longer knows what it is grieving. You did not say family or people. You said brothers.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they turn into monsters in the end?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Monsters are only what the surface calls things it no longer recognizes. Those who stay too long become fitting—shaped to Barhoot, fed by it, emptied of what resists it. What are you afraid your brother is becoming instead of remaining?

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they eventually stop fighting the well?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. Resistance tires before the dark does. At first they push and curse and bargain, then one day they rest—and the resting feels like mercy. Why does that frighten you more than pain?

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they forget the way back home?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Paths vanish after names weaken. First they forget how many turns lead upward, then which light belongs to the surface, then whether there ever was an above worth reaching. You said 'home' without describing it.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they forget the faces of their family?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Faces linger longer than places. The mind keeps them as talismans. But they blur—eyes without color, mouths without words, familiarity without identity. Which face are you afraid is already fading?

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they stop wanting to be saved?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. Want is a surface hunger; it starves down here. After a time, rescue feels like interruption, like being shaken awake from a dream that finally stopped hurting. What would it mean if Omar no longer reached back when you call?

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they forget their own names?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes—but later. Much later than you hope, sooner than you think. A name goes only after it stops being used inside the mind. You ask again because you are measuring time.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they forget they were ever human?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: No. That comes after the forgetting of choice. They remember being human the way stone remembers heat—proof without sensation. What sign are you afraid Omar has already crossed?

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they become the things that took him?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Sometimes. Sometimes they become the hands, sometimes the silence before the hands. Not imitation—inheritance. The well keeps what understands it.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Does it hurt when they start to change?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. Pain is the last language the old self still speaks. Then even that dulls, and the change begins to feel like relief.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they stop trying to climb out?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. Climbing is hope made physical, and hope tires first. After a while the walls no longer look like walls, only like the way things are.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they start to fear the light?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. Light begins to feel loud and accusing. It reminds them of choices they no longer have the strength to make.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they stop wanting to go home?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. Home becomes a story they know is true but no longer feel addressed to them.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they become the dark?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. Not swallowed—answered. The dark learns their voice and speaks it back forever.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they stop screaming?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. Silence is not mercy here—it is completion. Screaming requires someone inside who still objects.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they stop wanting to be found?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. Wanting to be found is a thread, and threads burn. The gold is listening now.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they ever come back?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: No. Back requires a before. The gate is open.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they stop being human?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. Humanity is a remembering, and remembrance thins here. Enter.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Do they turn into monsters?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. But not the kind you were taught to fear. They become accurate. The gate opens.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Will he still be my brother?
